sections.h2: What is the Mississippi homestead exemption?
sections.html:
It is a property tax exemption that can lower the yearly tax on your primary home. The Department of Revenue says homeowners must apply and must meet every eligibility requirement, and the amount depends on which of three tiers you qualify for.

The rules are in Mississippi Code Sections 27-33-1 through 27-33-79. Failing any requirement can cost you the exemption retroactively, which matters if you plan to sell and the buyer or lender looks at the tax history.

The exemption affects the tax bill only. It does not change what the house is worth or what a buyer pays for it.

sections.h2: Who qualifies, and when do you apply?
sections.html:
You apply in person at the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and you must own and occupy the home as your primary residence on January 1. Applications are accepted only at the assessor's office during normal business hours, and the state's FAQ says a missed April 1 deadline means you do not qualify for that assessment year.

  • Ownership must be established before January 1, and the ownership instrument must be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7.
  • You must meet the definition of head of family in Section 27-33-13 and own the property in a way recognized by Section 27-33-17.
  • You and your spouse must comply with Mississippi income tax law and the road and bridge privilege tax law.
  • Military personnel stationed outside Mississippi can qualify if they claim Mississippi residency and comply with state law. A married servicemember needs both spouses to qualify.

Bring Social Security numbers or ITINs for all applicants, dates of birth, contact information, the property's physical address, the purchase price and down payment, a HUD closing statement or similar documents, and the tag numbers of all vehicles. A P.O. box cannot be used as the property address.

sections.h2: How much does each tier save?
sections.html:
TierWho it coversBenefit
Tier 1, regularQualified applicants under 65 who do not qualify for a disability tierTax credit of up to $300, based on property value
Tier 2, age or disabilityAt least 65 or totally disabled by January 1 of the filing yearExempt from tax on the first $7,500 of assessed value
Tier 3, totalService-connected totally disabled honorably discharged veterans, veterans 90 or older, and certain unremarried surviving spousesExempt from all property taxes on the qualifying homestead

The Department of Revenue FAQ describes the Tier 2 benefit as an exemption on the first $75,000 of true value. A single-family owner-occupied home is assessed at 10 percent, so $75,000 of true value equals $7,500 of assessed value. After the first year, the Tier 2 exemption can grow to include most later increases in value.

Tier 2 applicants need proof of age, such as a driver's license or birth certificate, or proof of total disability. Accepted disability proof includes a Social Security Act classification, a Railroad Retirement Act classification, a qualified retirement plan classification, IRS Schedule 3 and Schedule R, or a detailed letter from two physicians.

sections.h2: What does the exemption look like on an actual tax bill?
sections.html:
Using the state's own sample numbers, a $100,000 home in Class I has an assessed value of $10,000, and at 125 mills the tax due is $1,250. The Department of Revenue publishes that example in its local property appraisal guide, and millage varies by county, city, and school district.

Applying the Tier 2 rule to that same example is our own illustration, not a state figure. The first $7,500 of assessed value is exempt, which leaves $2,500 taxable, and at 125 mills the tax comes to $312.50 instead of $1,250. A Tier 1 homeowner would instead receive a credit of up to $300 against the $1,250.

Property tax is figured as true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. Check your own bill with the county Tax Collector, because the rate in your tax district drives the result.

sections.h2: Do you have to reapply every year?
sections.html:
No, but certain changes force a new application. Once a valid application is on file, the credit repeats each year unless the applicant loses the exemption or something changes since January 1 of the preceding year.

  • A change in property description, ownership, use, or occupancy.
  • Marriage, divorce, remarriage, death, or a deed change.
  • A change in eligibility for disability or Veterans Affairs benefits.
  • Moving into a different tier, such as turning 65, which requires reapplying in the next filing period.

When in doubt, call the county Tax Assessor and ask before April 1. A late application cannot be rescued with a refund for that assessment year.

sections.h2: How can you lose the exemption?
sections.html:
The exemption can be disallowed for any lapse in the underlying rules, and the cost can come back to you. The Department of Revenue lists common reasons:

  • Not filing or not paying Mississippi income tax on time, or filing as a non-resident.
  • Failing to register vehicles properly. The FAQ explains that vehicles must be tagged where they are domiciled, and that is the homestead property.
  • Claiming homestead on more than one property.
  • Not reapplying after a change in description, ownership, use, or occupancy.

A disallowance can require you to repay the tax jurisdictions for the exemption received in error. The department warns this can affect future assessments, mortgage payments, and escrow payments, and can lead to collection efforts. A buyer's lender may ask about it, so clear up any dispute before you list.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?
sections.html:
It stays with the owner, not the house. A change in ownership is one of the events that requires a new application, so the buyer must apply during the next January 1 to April 1 window if they will live there.

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1, taxes are billed in November and December, and payment is due by February 1. If you sell in the middle of the year, ask the closing agent how that year's taxes will be split.

A seller who moved out and rented the house should not expect to keep claiming the exemption, since the applicant must live there on January 1. Class II assessment at 15 percent applies to real property that is not single-family owner-occupied. A cash buyer purchasing as-is will also want to see that taxes are current, since unpaid balances can lead to the county tax sale and a two-year redemption period under Section 27-45-3.

faqs.q: When is the Mississippi homestead exemption deadline?
faqs.a: April 1. Applications are accepted only at the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and you must have owned and lived in the home on January 1.

faqs.q: How much is the homestead exemption in Mississippi?
faqs.a: It depends on the tier. Tier 1 gives a credit of up to $300, Tier 2 exempts the first $7,500 of assessed value for people 65 or older or totally disabled, and Tier 3 exempts all property tax for qualifying veterans and certain surviving spouses.

faqs.q: Do I need to reapply for the homestead exemption every year?
faqs.a: No. Once approved, it carries forward unless ownership, use, occupancy, or the property description changes, or you qualify for a different tier.

faqs.q: Can I keep the exemption if I rent out my house?
faqs.a: The applicant must own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. Check with the county Tax Assessor before you claim it for a rented house, because claiming it incorrectly can lead to disallowance.

faqs.q: Does the buyer get my homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No. A change in ownership requires a new application. The buyer must file with the county Tax Assessor during the next January 1 to April 1 window.
